Mesopotamia

California History–Social Science 6.2

Mesopotamia means "the land between the rivers." It was between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in what is now mostly Iraq. These rivers could flood without warning, so farming was hard. Farmers dug canals to bring water to their fields. With more food, people could build some of the first cities in the world. The Sumerians lived in city-states like Uruk. Each city had its own ruler. A giant temple called a ziggurat stood at the center. Sumerian scribes needed to keep track of grain and trade, so they invented cuneiform, one of the first kinds of writing. Later, Sargon of Akkad took over the city-states and made the world's first empire. Hammurabi, a king of Babylon, wrote down 282 laws so everyone would know the rules. The Sumerians are also believed to have invented the wheel, the plow and the sailboat.
